title: normality
text: normality R package provides collection statistical tools assessing whether sample consistent normal distribution. includes: empirical distribution function (EDF)-based tests; moment-based tests; Shapiro-family tests; skewness kurtosis assessments; high-level automatic normality assessment

title: normality
text: formal normality tests use: \[H_0: X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\] versus \[H_1: X \\sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\] small p-value provides evidence normality. large p-value indicates test detect sufficient evidence departure normality. large p-value prove data normally distributed. Different tests sensitive different forms departure. example, skewness-based procedures focus asymmetry, kurtosis-based procedures focus tail weight, EDF procedures compare empirical theoretical distributions.

title: normality
text: high-level functions support data frames formulas. formula form: interface available is_normal(): samples fewer 8 observations, automatic assessment relies Shapiro–Wilk–Royston. samples 8 19 observations, combines: Shapiro–Wilk–Royston; skewness; Anderson–Darling. samples least 20 observations, combines: Shapiro–Wilk–Royston; D’Agostino–Pearson; Anderson–Darling. sensitivity argument controls many component assessments must support normality. allowed range 1 3. larger value makes criterion conservative.
code: data("iris") check_normality(iris, Sepal.Length ~ Species, method = "SWR") #>            x is_normal    Pvalue         W #> 1     setosa      TRUE 0.4595132 0.9776985 #> 2 versicolor      TRUE 0.4647370 0.9778357 #> 3  virginica      TRUE 0.2583148 0.9711794 #>                                    method #> 1 Shapiro-Wilk-Royston (w) normality test #> 2 Shapiro-Wilk-Royston (w) normality test #> 3 Shapiro-Wilk-Royston (w) normality test response ~ group out <- is_normal(iris, Sepal.Length ~ Species, summary = TRUE) set.seed(123) x1 <- c(rnorm(20), runif(10))  for (i in 1:3) {     res <- is_normal(x1, sensitivity = i)     print(sprintf("When sensitivity is %i: %s", i, res)) } #> [1] "When sensitivity is 1: TRUE" #> [1] "When sensitivity is 2: TRUE" #> [1] "When sensitivity is 3: FALSE"

title: Normality test — check_normality
text: method argument specifies statistical procedure used assess whether sample consistent normal distribution. Different tests emphasize different characteristics departures normality, skewness, kurtosis, discrepancies tails distribution. single test performs optimally circumstances, choice method may depend sample size expected type non-normality. Available methods : "AD": Anderson–Darling test. modification empirical distribution function (EDF) approach gives greater weight observations tails distribution. Compared several alternative normality tests, Anderson–Darling procedure often sensitive deviations occurring extreme values tail behavior. test applicable sample sizes n >= 8. "CVM": Cramér–von Mises test. empirical distribution function (EDF)-based goodness--fit test measures overall discrepancy empirical theoretical cumulative distribution functions assigning relatively uniform weight across entire distribution. Compared Anderson–Darling test, Cramér–von Mises test generally less sensitive deviations tails performs well detecting overall departures normality. test applicable sample sizes n >= 8. "DAP": D'Agostino–Pearson test. combined omnibus moment test based sample skewness kurtosis. procedure transforms skewness kurtosis statistics approximately standard normal variables combines single test statistic. method designed detect broad range departures normality rather emphasizing particular feature. test applicable sample sizes n >= 20. "JB": Jarque–Bera test. omnibus moment test based sample skewness kurtosis. test evaluates whether observed skewness kurtosis differ significantly values expected normal distribution. method commonly used econometrics generally appropriate moderate large sample sizes. "LF": Lilliefors test. Lilliefors test EDF omnibus test modified Kolmogorov-Smirnov test composite hypothesis normality. test statistic maximal absolute difference empirical hypothetical cumulative distribution function. "SW": Shapiro–Wilk test. original normality test proposed Shapiro Wilk (1965), based correlation ordered observations expected values normality. widely regarded one powerful tests detecting departures normality small samples. Applicable sample sizes 3 <= n <= 50. "SF": Shapiro–Francia test. Proposed Shapiro Francia (1972) subsequently simplified extended Royston (1993). method computationally simpler modification Shapiro–Wilk procedure performs particularly well detecting departures associated heavier-tailed distributions. Applicable sample sizes 5 <= n <= 5000. "SWR": Shapiro–Wilk test Royston's modifications. Uses Royston's (1992) approximations null distribution Shapiro–Wilk statistic extends applicability larger samples maintaining behavior similar original test. Applicable sample sizes 3 <= n <= 5000. methods, null hypothesis sample drawn normal distribution. Small p-values indicate evidence assumption normality.

text: method "SW": Shapiro–Wilk test, original normality test proposed Shapiro Wilk (1965). Applicable sample sizes 3 <= n <= 50.
